source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A Model of Case-based Planning (AAAI-86)
finding: Core theory. Failures are stored in memory next to successes. A failure is indexed by the features of the goals that together caused it. When those features show up in a new input, the planner is warned before it plans, and adds a goal 'avoid this failure'.
numbers: CHEF has six processes: anticipation, retrieval, modification, repair, credit assignment, storage. Example plan: 17 steps on about a dozen ingredients (chicken and peanuts).
quote: Memories of past failures are used to warn the planner of impending problems
limits: Single worked example, no test set, no error rates. Cooking domain, simulated world with hand-written causal rules.
agent_relevance: Store each lesson as (trap features -> warning), and check the warning BEFORE the attempt, not only after a failure.

source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A Model of Case-based Planning (AAAI-86) - the beef and broccoli failure
finding: The founding example. Stir-frying beef and broccoli together: liquid from the beef makes the broccoli soggy. The failure is indexed by three goal features (include meat, include a crisp vegetable, make a stir-fry). Later, a chicken and snow peas request has the same abstract features, so CHEF is reminded of the failure and avoids it.
numbers: Index = 3 features (meat, crisp vegetable, stir-fry). Retrieval drove down a discrimination network and found the repaired beef-and-broccoli plan, not the surface-closer chicken-and-green-beans plan.
quote: finds it on the basis of the prediction of this problem, even though the surface features of the two situations are dissimilar
limits: The reminding works because the feature vocabulary (goal types) was hand-chosen to capture the interaction. Surface similarity alone would have picked the wrong plan.
agent_relevance: A lesson must be indexed by the abstract conditions that cause the trap, not by the surface topic of the task. Surface retrieval can fetch the wrong case.

source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A Model of Case-based Planning (AAAI-86) - plan repair through causal explanation
finding: After simulating a plan, CHEF builds a causal explanation of the failure by back-chaining from the failed state to the steps that caused it. The explanation selects one of 20 known TOPs (Thematic Organization Packets). Each TOP holds general repair strategies.
numbers: 20 TOPs known. The beef/broccoli failure maps to SIDE-EFFECT:DISABLED-CONDITION:CONCURRENT. Three strategies attach: SPLIT-AND-REFORM, ALTER-PLAN:SIDE-EFFECT, ADJUNCT-PLAN. Only SPLIT-AND-REFORM was feasible, so the beef and broccoli were stir-fried apart and joined at the end.
quote: The explanation of the failure in this example indexes to the TOP SIDE-EFFECT:DISABLED-CONDITION:CONCURRENT
limits: Repair quality depends on the hand-built causal rule base. Failure detection is by a simulator, not the real world.
agent_relevance: Explanation chooses the repair class. In our schema this is G2: a revision must cite the real failing output, and the explanation type picks the fix.

source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A Model of Case-based Planning (AAAI-86) - credit assignment
finding: CHEF uses the causal explanation to decide which input features to blame, and links only those to the failure memory (a marker-passing demon under MEAT and VEGETABLE). This turns one failure into a rule that predicts future failures.
numbers: One failure produced two demons: 'meat sweats when stir-fried' and 'stir-frying in too much liquid makes crisp vegetables soggy'.
quote: the planner wants to repair the characterization of the world that allowed it to create the failed plan in the first place
limits: Blame is correct only if the causal model is correct. A wrong explanation would index the lesson under the wrong features and mis-fire later.
agent_relevance: The trap in 'lessons with traps': a wrong explanation poisons the index. Check the explanation against another test before storing the lesson.

source: Hammond (1986) CHEF: A Model of Case-based Planning (AAAI-86) - plan storage by problems avoided
finding: A repaired plan is stored under the goals it meets AND the problems it avoids. So a predicted problem retrieves a plan that already solved it.
numbers: Repaired beef-and-broccoli plan indexed under stir fry, beef, and 'avoids soggy vegetable'.
quote: indexed by the goals they satisfy and the problems they avoid
limits: Needs a fixed vocabulary of problem names. New kinds of trap have no index until credit assignment creates one.
agent_relevance: Keep fixes together with the trap they solve, so one lookup returns both warning and cure.

source: Riesbeck (1981) Failure-driven reminding for incremental learning (IJCAI-81)
finding: First formal use of failure-driven reminding. When a comprehension rule fails, the failure and its fix are stored as an exception episode attached to the rule. The rule itself is not changed. Later failures of that rule retrieve the stored episodes. The rule is rewritten only when the exceptions can be grouped into a class.
numbers: ALFRED program, hand-analysed input. Example: '$55 billion' judged large, then shown small next to $1.23 trillion; later '100,000 barrels' judged large next to 6 million barrels per day. Reminded of the first error, the learner caught the second.
quote: Subsequent failures of that rule trigger the retrieval of these exception episodes
limits: Preliminary program, no classification scheme for exceptions, no quantitative test. The author notes a rule with known problems may still add plausible wrong beliefs.
agent_relevance: Do not rewrite a general rule after one failure. Tag it with the episode and retrieve the episode when the rule is doubted again (fits G1 doubt only on a signal).

source: Riesbeck (1981) - lesson scope
finding: The learner changes with expertise: everyday rules (big number = big effect) are replaced by cautious rules such as 'do not assume, find out', and relative size is judged only once explicit comparison points exist.
numbers: Rule is kept in use after its first failure, and only questioned when another problem arises.
limits: Domain-specific: the everyday rule stays valid outside economics, so the lesson is scoped to a domain.
agent_relevance: A lesson needs a scope tag. 'Postpone judging until a reference point exists' is a reusable guard for estimation tasks.

source: Schank (1982) Dynamic Memory: A Theory of Reminding and Learning in Computers and People
finding: Schank's claim: memory is failure-driven. When an expectation fails, the failure is noted, a reminding to an earlier similar failure is triggered, and the memory structure is re-organised. Understanding and learning are one process. Book not opened this session; account from secondary sources (search results on Schank-Leake 1989).
numbers: No numbers; theory book.
limits: Not opened. Secondary description only. Theory, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Basis for the idea that expectation failure is the trigger for storing a lesson, matching our rule to learn only from a real signal.

source: Schank and Leake (1989) Creativity and learning in a case-based explainer (Artificial Intelligence 40)
finding: SWALE detects anomalies, explains them by retrieving old explanation patterns (XPs) and tweaking them, then installs the new explanation in memory. Authors cite failure-driven reminding as a main influence. Full PDF was blocked (IP access denied); only the abstract and secondary accounts seen.
numbers: Example anomaly: racehorse Swale died after a light gallop.
limits: Not opened as full text. Explanations were built by hand-coded tweak strategies and evaluated by program heuristics.
agent_relevance: An explanation is a case too. Keep explanations of failures as reusable, revisable objects.

source: Leake - SWALE project page (Indiana University)
finding: Describes SWALE's three steps: retrieve XPs from other deaths, tweak them to fit, evaluate and store the best. Failed tweaks are kept as a resource: they open new options for more revision. Tweaking continues while each tweak improves the explanation.
numbers: 3 example remindings gave 6 explanations: Jim Fixx (1), Janis Joplin (2), 'too much sex will kill you' (3). Some were 'quite fanciful or can be ruled out'.
quote: Their revisions will not always be successful, but failures produce new possibilities for still more revision.
limits: Tiny demonstration. Library size not stated. Candidate quality judged by program heuristics, not independent tests.
agent_relevance: Generated explanations of a failure can be fanciful. They need a test before being stored as lessons (G3, G8).

source: Hammond (1986) Case-based planning, Yale PhD thesis (DTIC ADA180271) and Hammond (1989) Case-Based Planning book
finding: Thesis abstract (via search snippet) says the theory improves planning in three areas: failure avoidance, plan repair and plan reuse. DTIC download returned an HTML error page, so the text was not read.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as the AAAI-86 paper; the thesis is the full account.

source: Hammond (1990) Explaining and repairing plans that fail (Artificial Intelligence 45)
finding: Extended CHEF/repair account: plan failures are described by causal explanations, and the detail of the explanation guides which repair applies. Abstract level only.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened beyond abstract snippet.
agent_relevance: Supports using the explanation to select the repair.

source: Kolodner (1993) Case-Based Reasoning (book) - failure-driven learning
finding: Standard text that treats failure as a retention trigger: store the failed case with its explanation, repair, and the indices that would have predicted the failure. Book not opened. Listed because the task names Kolodner.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; description from general knowledge of the field, treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Textbook source for the design of a failure case record.

source: Riesbeck and Schank (1989/1998) Inside Case-Based Reasoning - micro CHEF
finding: Secondary page describing micro CHEF (page 164): adaptation, failure prediction, failure repair. Same beef-and-green-bean to beef-and-broccoli case. Author also reports a chatbot gave plausible causes of soggy broccoli but missed the broth explanation.
numbers: One chat test, no numbers.
limits: Blog-level source. Anecdote only.
agent_relevance: Shows the explanation, not the symptom, is the valuable part.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Modern LLM version of failure-driven memory. After a failed trial the model writes a verbal reflection that is added to a small memory and used in the next attempt.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. AlfWorld: 130 of 134 tasks solved with ReAct+Reflexion, +22% absolute over 12 trials. HotPotQA +20%. Memory kept to a sliding window of 3 experiences.
limits: Needs a repeatable task and an environment signal. ReAct-only AlfWorld gains stalled between trials 6 and 7. Reflection quality not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Direct template for failure notes. Window of 3 is a small, deliberate memory.

source: Reflexion - ablation of self-reflection
finding: On HotPotQA with ground-truth context, adding the self-reflection step beat plain episodic memory (most recent trajectory) by 8% absolute. So the written explanation adds value over raw failed trajectory.
numbers: 8% absolute over episodic-memory-only, 100 HotPotQA questions.
quote: self-reflection improves learning by an 8% absolute boost over the episodic memory learning advantage
limits: Single task type, 100 questions, no repeat seeds reported.
agent_relevance: Raw failure traces are worse than failure traces with an explanation. This supports 'keep failures WITH explanations'.

source: Reflexion - test generation ablation and the false-positive trap
finding: Without internal unit tests, Reflexion got worse than baseline. Without the natural-language explanation step it did no better than baseline. On MBPP Python, Reflexion lost to plain GPT-4 because internal tests passed wrong code.
numbers: Rust, 50 hardest HumanEval: 52% without test generation vs 60% baseline. False-positive test rate: MBPP Python 16.3%, HumanEval Python 1.4%. Baseline pass@1 82% (HumanEval) and 80% (MBPP).
quote: the agent is unable to determine if the current implementation is correct without unit tests
limits: Small subset (50 problems). Authors' own analysis.
agent_relevance: The trap: when the failure signal is a false positive, the lesson is wrong. Matches G3: a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to.

source: Reflexion - hallucination loop in AlfWorld
finding: Baseline agents often believe they hold an item they do not. Without long-term memory the hallucination rate stayed at 22% with no recovery.
numbers: 22% hallucination rate, 134 tasks.
limits: Heuristic detector for hallucination and inefficient planning.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-side detector (repeat actions, impossible state) can trigger the failure note.

source: Zhao et al. (2023/2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners (AAAI 2024)
finding: ExpeL gathers success and failure trajectories, then extracts cross-task insights by comparing a failed and a successful run of the same task (operations ADD, EDIT, UPVOTE, DOWNVOTE). Insights are applied at test time with no retries.
numbers: HotpotQA: insights-only 36%, retrieval-only 31%. ALFWorld: 50% vs 55%. WebShop 37% vs 38%. ExpeL 40% at trial 3 vs Reflexion 39% on HotpotQA; ALFWorld 54% vs Reflexion 59%. Four-fold validation.
limits: Reflexion is better on ALFWorld. Insight extractor depends on GPT-4; gpt-3.5 extractor was worse. Needs diverse success/failure pairs.
agent_relevance: Compare a failure against a success of the same task to write the lesson; vote lessons up or down so wrong ones die.

source: ExpeL ablations - what hurts the lessons
finding: Learned insights beat hand-written ones. Adding Reflexion-style reflections into insight extraction HURT, probably because reflections sometimes hallucinate. Insights from the few-shot examples only gave no gain over ReAct. Experience from Reflexion retries beat experience from ReAct without retries.
numbers: HotpotQA ablation table 3; random example selection dropped sharply; ranking by reason similarity also dipped.
quote: using reflections in addition to success/failure pairs and lists of successes is disadvantageous
limits: Single environment (HotpotQA) for insight ablations.
agent_relevance: A wrong reflection poisons later lessons. Do not feed unverified explanations into the lesson store.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025/2026) ReasoningBank
finding: Memory items distilled from BOTH self-judged successes and failures (title, description, content; at most 3 items per trajectory). Failures yield preventative lessons. Plus memory-aware test-time scaling.
numbers: WebArena overall success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 over no-memory for three backbones; up to 20% relative gain and 16% fewer steps. Shopping subset, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 39.0; success-only memory 46.5, with failures 49.7.
quote: unlike the baselines, ReasoningBank can transform failures into constructive signals rather than noise
limits: Other memories got no benefit from failures: Synapse 40.6 to 41.7, AWM 44.4 to 42.2 (worse). Judge accuracy 72.7% against ground truth.
agent_relevance: Failures only help if they are distilled into a strategy-level lesson. Raw failed traces added to a success-only store can hurt.

source: ReasoningBank - robustness to a noisy failure judge
finding: Gains held when the judge that labels success or failure was 70-90% accurate; best with 100% ground truth. The test went down to 50% (random).
numbers: Judge accuracy simulated from 50% to 100%; real judge 72.7%. Shopping subset only.
limits: One subset, one backbone for this test. Result at 50% not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Failure labels from a model judge are usable but should be code-checked where possible (G2, G5).

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Memento: Fine-tuning LLM agents without fine-tuning LLMs
finding: Case-based reasoning agent with a case bank of (state, action, reward) triples that keeps both successes and failures; retrieval by similarity or a learned Q-function. Framed as a memory-augmented MDP.
numbers: GAIA validation 87.88% pass@3, test 79.40%. DeepResearcher 66.6 F1 / 80.4 PM; CBR adds 4.7 to 9.6 points on out-of-distribution tasks. Best retrieval count K=4; larger K plateaus or declines. Five learning rounds: 78.65 (no CBR) to 84.47; 79.84 to 84.85 (non-parametric); 80.46 to 85.44 (parametric).
limits: Planner is GPT-4.1 and executor o3 or o4-mini, so gains are mixed with strong tools. Failures kept as cases but not studied apart from successes.
agent_relevance: Retrieve few cases (about 4). More cases add noise, unlike few-shot prompts.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-repair gains are small once compute cost is counted, because the model is bad at explaining its own failure. A stronger model or a human giving the explanation raises repair success a lot.
numbers: GPT-4 explanation vs human explanation, repair success: overall 33.30% vs 52.60%; introductory 42.64% vs 62.21%; interview 19.33% vs 45.67%; competition 3.67% vs 14.67%. On APPS GPT-4 beat baseline by up to 8%; GPT-3.5 gains marginal.
quote: self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on its own code
limits: Code tasks, HumanEval and APPS, small human study.
agent_relevance: The explanation of a failure is the weak step, not the fix. Matches the schema line: models find errors poorly but fix them well once shown.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to critique and revise often lowers accuracy. Oracle-label stopping creates the apparent gains in earlier papers.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7 over two rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3. 74.7% of GSM8K answers unchanged.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
limits: Reasoning tasks, two models, prompts from earlier papers.
agent_relevance: A failure lesson must come from a real failure signal, never from the model's own opinion that it failed (G2).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Exploring the use of negative trajectories in agent tuning (NAT)
finding: Fine-tuning with failed trajectories, marked by a prefix or suffix saying the trajectory failed, improves over positive-only data. Quality of negatives matters.
numbers: 2k positives + 10k negatives: improvement -3.16 with low-quality negatives vs +8.74 with high-quality ones. Action error rate in training data 4.01% (positive only) vs 15.33% with negatives. Math CoT: +6.68% over no-negative training.
limits: Fine-tuning, not scaffolding. Gain shrinks as positives grow.
agent_relevance: Failures help only when labelled as failures and of good quality. Unlabelled failures teach errors.

source: LEMA: Learning from mistakes makes LLM better reasoner
finding: Fine-tune on (mistake, explanation, correction) triples made by GPT-4 from the model's own wrong solutions. Gains are modest but consistent.
numbers: LLaMA-2-70B GSM8K 83.5 vs 81.4 (CoT data only); MATH 25.0 vs 23.6. Across five models gains of +0.3 to +4.6 points. 50 corrections hand-graded for quality.
limits: Needs a stronger model to write the corrections. Fine-tuning, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Mistake plus explanation plus fix is the useful unit, as in CHEF.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Where LLM agents fail and how they can learn from failures (AgentDebug)
finding: Taxonomy of agent errors (memory, reflection, planning, action, system) and a 200-trajectory annotated benchmark (100 ALFWorld, 50 WebShop, 50 GAIA, 10 annotators). AgentDebug finds the earliest root-cause step, then gives targeted feedback and the agent retries.
numbers: All-correct accuracy 24.3% vs 0.3% for best baseline; step accuracy 45.0% vs 28.0%. ALFWorld success: GPT-4o-mini 21 to 55, Qwen3-8B 48 to 74, Qwen3-Next-80B 60 to 84. Up to 26% relative task gain.
limits: Retry needs a repeatable task. Root-cause judge quality depends on the base model (GPT-4.1 best).
agent_relevance: Look for the EARLIEST error, because early mistakes cascade. Store the root cause, not the last symptom.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Trajectory-informed memory generation for self-improving agent systems (IBM)
finding: Extracts strategy, recovery and optimisation tips with causal attribution of failures to decisions, stores them with provenance, injects them at run time. AppWorld.
numbers: Test-normal: task goal completion 73.2% vs 69.6% baseline (+3.6 pp); scenario goal completion 64.3% vs 50.0% (+14.3 pp). Cosine threshold 0.6 gave 72.0% / 62.5%; top-3 restriction fell below baseline (66.7% / 48.2%). Difficulty-1 train tasks at 100% baseline fell to 94.4% with tips.
limits: Small test set; tips hurt on tasks the agent already solved.
agent_relevance: Advice can hurt where the agent is already right. Gate lesson injection to cases where it matches closely.

source: Su et al. (2026) Mistake Notebook Learning: batch-clustered failures
finding: Cluster failures in a batch, write shared mistake notes, and commit a memory update only if batch accuracy improves, otherwise roll back.
numbers: Text-to-SQL KaggleDBQA on DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp: 24.0% to 64.0% with 54 entries and 514 guidance tokens; ACE 54.0% with 9406 tokens. Qwen3-8B 19.0% to 28.0%. Qwen3-Max 40.0% to 46.0%.
limits: Small SQL test sets. Some interactive-agent rows showed no gain.
agent_relevance: Accept a new lesson only if it improves a held-out batch (G3, G7). This is a gate for lessons with traps.
